title: Tektronix 492 Spectrum Analyzer
subtitle: A microprocessor-controlled portable spectrum analyzer whose marker cursors and GPIB computer linkage made the frequency domain a direct, queryable interface.
why_scout_cares: The museum has oscilloscopes and logic analyzers but no spectrum analyzer — this opens the frequency-domain instrument class. The 492's digital readout overlaid on the CRT graticule, front-panel marker/cursor controls, and IEEE-488 (GPIB) remote computer programming make it a real computer-linked measurement interface, distinct from the existing Tektronix oscilloscopes.

research.title: Tektronix 492 Spectrum Analyzer
research.overview:
The Tektronix 492, introduced in 1978 (with the higher-bandwidth 496 following in 1983), was a portable, microprocessor-controlled spectrum analyzer that dominated the lab spectrum-analyzer market for a decade. It is a genuinely different instrument class from the oscilloscopes already in the museum: instead of displaying a time-domain waveform, it sweeps a frequency spectrum and renders it on a large analog CRT.

The 492's HCI-relevant features are the digital frequency readout drawn directly onto the CRT graticule (rather than a separate display), the front-panel marker and cursor controls that let the operator place a marker on the trace and read frequency/amplitude directly, and full IEEE-488 (GPIB) remote programming and data transfer so a host computer could drive the instrument and receive trace data. This computer linkage is the defining 'measurement instrument with a host' behavior of the era.

A dense two-tier front panel of concentric coarse/fine tuning knobs and pushbutton functions exemplifies the 'every control has its own knob, read out digitally on screen' interaction style — the archetype of professional lab instrumentation before menu-driven soft-key UIs arrived.

deepDive.heading: Marker-cursor interaction
deepDive.text: Front-panel delta-marker and peak/marker pushbuttons let the operator set and read frequency and amplitude directly off the displayed trace. This is a primitive marker/soft-key grammar: you point at a feature of the spectrum and the machine tells you its value.

deepDive.heading: Computer linkage via GPIB
deepDive.text: Standard IEEE-488 (GPIB) remote programming and data transfer meant the 492 could be driven by a controller and return trace data to it — the defining 'lab instrument with a host computer' behavior, connecting the analog front end to a general-purpose computer.

deepDive.heading: Digital readout on the graticule
deepDive.text: Frequency, span, and reference-level values were drawn as digital alphanumeric text directly onto the CRT graticule rather than on a separate LED readout — an early instance of merging numeric state into the displayed signal itself.
